title: Benchmarking Zero-Setup Quantum Circuit Simulators
authors: Arul Rhik Mazumder, Mohammed Zuhair Mullath, Hayk Tepanyan
abstract: Practitioners increasingly rely on hosted simulation environments, but their performance characteristics remain poorly documented. We present a systematic benchmarking study of GPU-accelerated approximate quantum simulation across two widely used methods: matrix product states (MPS) and Pauli path simulation (PPS), comparing BlueQubit (a hosted tool that handles hardware provisioning, simulator configuration, and job orchestration) against AWS Braket, Quantum Rings, PPS-Qiskit, and PauliPropagation.jl. For MPS, we find that GPU runtime yields sub-quadratic scaling with bond dimension, with a growing advantage over CPU at increasing scale. For Pauli path simulation on IBM's 127-qubit kicked Ising benchmark, GPUs deliver up to $1{,}400\times$ speedup at fine truncation thresholds ($δ= 2.5 \times 10^{-5}$, 27.6M Pauli terms), and are the only backends that reach accuracy regimes below $δ= 10^{-5}$, which remained inaccessible to the commodity CPU-based implementations and self-contained SDKs evaluated here. We also provide a reproducible characterization of these simulators across regimes, including tradeoffs that isolated evaluations do not show. To support transparency and reuse, we provide a public GitHub repository containing all benchmarking code and configurations.
summary: This paper conducts a comprehensive benchmark of various hosted quantum circuit simulators, comparing performance across GPU-accelerated MPS and PPS methods against state-of-the-art backends. The key finding is that GPUs offer massive speedups, enabling simulations at higher accuracy and scale than previously possible using commodity CPUs. It establishes a standardized protocol for evaluating the practical computational limits of current quantum simulation toolkits.
main_problem: The performance characteristics of hosted quantum circuit simulation environments are poorly documented, making it difficult for practitioners to select an optimal backend.
main_result: GPU acceleration provides substantial speedups (up to 1,400x) over CPU implementations for both MPS and PPS simulations, enabling access to higher accuracy regimes previously unreachable.
method: The study systematically benchmarks multiple zero-setup simulators (BlueQubit, AWS Braket, etc.) across different simulation methods: State-Vector (SV), Matrix Product States (MPS), and Pauli Path Simulation (PPS).
model_or_system: Quantum circuits are simulated using various approximation techniques. Benchmarks include random SU(4) circuits, Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT), and the 127-qubit kicked Ising model.
key_observables: Runtime ($T$), speedup factor ($S$), scaling exponents ($\chi$ for MPS), and simulation accuracy/fidelity ($\delta$).
important_parameters: Bond dimension ($\chi$), qubit count ($n$), circuit depth ($d$), and truncation threshold ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The comparison relies on standardized protocols to expose crossover points, but limitations include the scope of vendor APIs (e.g., AWS Braket SV1) and the exclusion of hybrid variational workloads.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dramatic runtime divergence between GPU and CPU backends for state-vector simulation at high qubit counts ($\ge 30$), and show scaling behavior for MPS/PPS methods.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a systematic benchmarking study, comparing multiple software tools across different physical simulation regimes (SV, MPS, PPS) to provide reproducible performance characterizations.
why_interesting: It provides crucial, quantitative data on the computational scaling of modern quantum simulation techniques (MPS/PPS), which are essential numerical tools for studying strongly correlated systems and dynamics in condensed matter physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Log-scale runtime (ms) for quantum volume circuits on CPU (solid blue) and GPU (dashed red) across 16–34 qubits and five circuit depths (30–150). GPU outperforms CPU by 1–2 orders of magnitude at higher qubit counts; both scale exponentially. The dip at 29 qubits on CPU curves reflects a hardware transition in the managed platform.

Fig. 2: Quantum volume circuit runtime at depth 60 across four backends (16–34 qubits, log scale). BlueQubit GPU (red) is fastest at all qubit counts, reaching ∼4 × 104 ms at 34 qubits. BlueQubit CPU (blue) exhibits a characteristic dip near 29 qubits before resuming exponential growth. Braket SV1 (purple) diverges sharply above 27 qubits, surpassing 107 ms above 30 qubits; benchmarking was discontinued beyond 31 qubits due to excessive runtime and cloud cost. Quantum Rings (green) and BlueQubit CPU converge near 106 ms at 34 qubits.

Fig. 3: MPS runtime vs. bond dimension at n = 40 qubits, d = 10 layers (log–log scale). CPU scaling (T ∝χ2.03±0.11) approaches the theoretical χ2 for gate-contraction-dominated regimes. GPU scaling (T ∝χ1.49±0.06) is sub-quadratic, reflecting efficient parallelization of contraction and SVD operations at large tensor sizes. The GPU advantage grows with χ as S(χ) ∝χ0.55. Dotted lines extrapolate both fits to χ = 5,000, projecting runtimes of 119.2 h (CPU) vs. 11.7 h (GPU).

Figure 2 compares all four state-vector backends on the same depth-60 QV circuits. Three findings emerge. First, BlueQubit GPU is the fastest state-vector backend at all tested qubit counts, outperforming Braket SV1 and Quantum Rings by 1–2 orders of magnitude at 30+ qubits and BlueQubit CPU by roughly 2× at 34 qubits.
